summary: Describes Lemonade, a profile of IMAP, mail submission and Sieve that helps constrained clients, such as mobile devices with limited memory or bandwidth, use email efficiently. It lists required extensions, restrictions and usage modes.

plainLanguage.summary: Lemonade is a list of what a mail server must support so that a small client, such as one on a phone, can work cheaply over a slow link. It covers saving and resuming drafts without moving the whole message each time, telling the client about new mail, and forwarding an attachment without sending its contents through the phone.

subtitle: A checklist of IMAP, mail submission and Sieve extensions that lets phones and other small clients handle email cheaply.

tldr.problem: Email clients on phones and other constrained devices waste bandwidth and time on the standard protocols. A draft is saved and fetched again in full, a forwarded attachment is downloaded and uploaded, and a dropped connection forces a full resynchronization.
tldr.mechanism: Lemonade is a profile that names the extensions a server must offer: quick resynchronization, server-side message part handling, notifications, and a forwarding scheme in which the mail server fetches the parts of a message directly from the store instead of the client uploading them.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5550 is a Proposed Standard from August 2009 that obsoletes RFC 4550 and updates RFC 4469 and RFC 4467. Compared with the earlier profile it adds more required IMAP extensions, two new IMAP keywords, and the Sieve filtering language with its extensions.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
The Lemonade Profile, or simply Lemonade, provides enhancements to Internet email to support diverse service environments. A Lemonade mail server provides both a Lemonade Submission Server and a Lemonade Message Store, which are based on the existing Mail Submission and IMAP protocols respectively, and MAY also include a Lemonade Message Delivery Agent, which provides delivery-time filtering services based on Sieve.

The profile includes general common enhancements to Internet Mail, described in Sections 4 and 5; "forward without download", which describes exchanges between Lemonade clients and servers that allow a new message to be submitted with content that resides outside the client, described in Section 8; quick mailbox resynchronization, described in Section 5.1; extensions to support more precise and broader notifications from the store, described in Sections 5.4.1 and 5.5; and delivery-time filtering for typical mail management use cases.

The working group used the architecture described in RFC 5442 to develop the profile, and it is intended to support realizations of the Open Mobile Alliance's mobile email enabler using Internet Mail protocols defined by the IETF. The document uses the terminology of RFC 5598 on email architecture, and in its examples the letters M, I and S mark lines sent by the client, the IMAP server and the SMTP submit server.
sections.plainLanguage: Lemonade names three roles for a mail server: the part that accepts outgoing mail, the part that stores mail, and optionally the part that filters mail as it arrives. The profile lists what each role must do so that a small client can work within a small budget.

sections.title: Summary of Required Support
sections.content:
A Lemonade Submission Server MUST provide the service described in the Mail Submission protocol and MUST support the SMTP extensions 8BITMIME, AUTH, BINARYMIME, BURL with the imap option, CHUNKING, DSN, ENHANCEDSTATUSCODES, PIPELINING, SIZE and STARTTLS. The profile imposes further requirements in some cases, detailed in Section 4.

A Lemonade Message Store MUST provide the service described in IMAP and MUST support the IMAP extensions BINARY, CATENATE, COMPRESS=DEFLATE, CONDSTORE, CONTEXT=SEARCH, CONTEXT=SORT, CONVERT, ENABLE, ESEARCH, ESORT, I18NLEVEL=1, IDLE, LITERAL+, NAMESPACE, NOTIFY, QRESYNC, SASL-IR, SORT, STARTTLS, UIDPLUS and URLAUTH, plus URL-PARTIAL as described in Section 5.7.1. The store MUST also store the $Forwarded, $SubmitPending and $Submitted keywords. In addition to that list, every Lemonade Message Store MUST send the CAPABILITY response code in the initial server greeting and after the LOGIN and AUTHENTICATE commands.

A Lemonade Message Delivery Agent MUST support the Sieve mail filtering language and the Sieve extensions ENOTIFY, IMAP4FLAGS, RELATIONAL, VACATION and VARIABLES, and the comparator-i;unicode-casemap comparator. It should also consider supporting a Sieve script management protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the checklist itself. The submitting server needs to accept binary mail, pipeline commands, report the size limit and tell the client when something went wrong. The store needs to resynchronize quickly, notify the client of changes, search efficiently and hand out URLs for stored messages. The delivery agent needs the filtering language and its common extensions.

sections.title: Message Store Behaviour
sections.content:
Resynchronization is a costly part of an IMAP session, and mobile networks are generally more prone to unintended disconnection, which makes the problem more acute. Lemonade Message Stores therefore MUST support CONDSTORE, QRESYNC and ENABLE, which let a client resynchronize any mailbox quickly by asking the server to return all flag changes and expunges since a previously recorded state. This also speeds up reconnection when the transport layer is cut.

Message parts, especially attachments, are a challenge for limited devices in both bandwidth and capability. The BINARY extension moves MIME body part decoding from the client to the server, and the decoded data is equal to or less in size than the encoded representation, so it reduces bandwidth. Servers SHALL always accept binary encoded MIME messages in APPEND commands for any folder. The CONVERT extension lets clients request conversions between media types, including scaling images, which lets a client view an attachment without coping with a wide range of media types.

For compression, stores SHOULD support the Deflate algorithm for TLS, but the working group acknowledges that this is rarely deployed, so stores MUST provide the IMAP COMPRESS extension for fallback application-level stream compression.

The addition of server-to-client notifications turns the profile into an event-based synchronization protocol. When the client is connected, inband notifications are generated: stores MUST support IDLE, which lets a client receive unsolicited notifications about changes in the selected mailbox without polling, and they also provide NOTIFY, which lets a client ask for specific event types to be sent immediately, such as message delivery and mailbox renames. When the client is not connected, the notification filter generates an outband notification, which may be considered as acting on a push email repository; if outband notification is disabled, the client must perform a quick-sync on reconnect using the resynchronization mechanisms.

Stores MUST support ESEARCH, which lets clients efficiently find the first or last matching messages, count matches and obtain a list of matches in a compact form. To avoid handling an entire mailbox, stores MUST implement CONTEXT=SEARCH, ESORT and CONTEXT=SORT, along with SORT. For mailbox handling, stores MUST support NAMESPACE, which lets clients discover shared mailboxes and mailboxes belonging to other users, and I18NLEVEL with a value of 1 or 2, which adds support for internationalized search and sort; because I18NLEVEL=2 implies support for I18NLEVEL=1, a client that uses the extension MUST recognize either one.

Three keywords are registered. The $Forwarded keyword marks a message that was forwarded to another address, embedded within or attached to a new message; once set, the flag SHOULD NOT be cleared, stores MUST preserve it on the COPY operation and servers MUST support SEARCH KEYWORD $Forwarded. The $SubmitPending keyword designates a message as awaiting submission, and $Submitted is added atomically with STORE (UNCHANGEDSINCE) when a client starts sending it; once submission succeeds, $SubmitPending is atomically cleared. The two keywords let a message being actively submitted be told apart from one waiting to be sent, and they let all messages that were supposed to be sent be found even if the client crashes before sending them.
sections.plainLanguage: Three things are meant to save traffic. The store can tell the client exactly what changed since the client last looked, so a reconnection costs one exchange rather than a full scan. The store can decode and convert message parts itself, so the client does not have to receive the original encoding. And the store can push news of a change to the client instead of waiting to be polled.

sections.title: Message Delivery Agents and Sieve
sections.content:
Lemonade Message Delivery Agents MUST support the Sieve filtering language at the point of delivery, allowing the user to control which messages are accepted and where they are filed.

Six Sieve extensions are required. VACATION lets the client set up an auto-responder. ENOTIFY lets a Sieve script generate notifications, such as by XMPP, SIP or email, about received messages. VARIABLES adds support for variables to the scripting language, typically used with Enotify or Vacation to customize responses and notifications. RELATIONAL adds relational comparisons to the language, typically used together with Enotify. IMAP4FLAGS lets a Sieve script set IMAP flags and keywords when delivering a message to a mailbox, for example to mark certain messages as interesting or urgent. The i;unicode-casemap comparator, declared as comparator-i;unicode-casemap in the Sieve require statement, allows case-insensitive matching of Unicode characters.
sections.plainLanguage: The delivery agent runs the user's own filtering rules on arriving mail. The rules can sort mail into folders, answer automatically when the user is away, and notify another program about a message.

sections.title: Message User Agent Requirements
sections.content:
All existing IMAP clients are Lemonade compliant in as much as all Lemonade services are based on the existing IMAP and Mail Submission protocols, but client implementors are encouraged to take full advantage of the facilities provided by Lemonade servers.

When opening a connection to the Submission Server, clients MUST do so using port 587 unless explicitly configured to use an alternate port. The RFC notes that this requirement is somewhat stronger than the one in the Mail Submission specification, which did not prescribe the exact procedure. If the TCP connection to port 587 fails to open, the client MAY then immediately retry using a different port, such as 25.

Clients SHOULD support the Format and DelSp parameters to the text/plain media type, as described in RFC 3676, and generate this format for messages, and they SHOULD support and use the $Forwarded keyword.
sections.plainLanguage: The client is told to submit mail on the standard submission port and to mark messages it has forwarded. Clients written against the ordinary IMAP and submission protocols still work; these are improvements to take up when possible.

sections.title: Forward without Download
sections.content:
The arrival of client/server email using IMAP and Submission turned what had been local disk operations into repetitive network data transmissions. Lemonade "forward without download" uses the SMTP BURL extension to reach external sources during submission, and in combination with the IMAP URLAUTH extension it makes it possible to include message parts, or even whole messages, from the IMAP store with a minimal trust relationship between the IMAP and SMTP submit servers. It keeps one submission protocol, so there is no risk of several parallel and possibly divergent mechanisms, and by keeping the details of submission in the submit server it can work with other retrieval protocols such as POP or NNTP.

The act of sending a message involves several steps: initiating a new draft, draft editing, message assembly and message submission. Initiation and editing take place in the client, and drafts are often saved to an IMAP server with the \Draft flag for later recall. Assembly produces the complete message from the final revision of the draft and external sources, retrieving and inserting external data. Submission inserts the assembled message into the SMTP infrastructure.

Traditionally, messages were initiated, edited and assembled entirely within the client, although drafts might be saved to an IMAP server and retrieved later, and the completed text was then transmitted to a Message Submission Agent. There was often no clear boundary between editing and assembly: if a message was forwarded, its content was retrieved immediately and inserted into the message text. As a consequence, each save of a draft and subsequent retrieval transmitted that entire content, as did submission.

Lemonade describes two ways of forwarding without downloading, depending on where assembly takes place. The first uses the extended APPEND command, CATENATE, to edit a draft message in the message store and cause the assembly to happen on the IMAP server; this is most often used when a copy of the message is to be retained on the IMAP server. The client uses CATENATE to create the message on the IMAP server from new text combined with one or more message parts already present there, uses UIDPLUS to learn the UID of the created message, and then obtains a URLAUTH format URL from the server with the GENURLAUTH command. That URL is given to the submit server in a BURL command, so the submit server fetches the content with URLFETCH. Without the LITERAL+ extension the new message is constructed using three round trips; with LITERAL+ it can be constructed using one.

The second uses a succession of BURL and BDAT commands to submit and assemble through concatenation. New body parts are supplied with BDAT commands and existing body parts are referenced with URLAUTH format URLs in BURL commands. In this variant the client asks for URLAUTH URLs for the pieces it wants to include, and the submit server fetches them with URLFETCH.

The "pawn-ticket" authorization mechanism uses a URI that contains its own authorization credentials. Its advantage is that the SMTP submit server cannot access any data on the URLAUTH server without a pawn-ticket created by the client; the pawn-ticket grants access only to the specific data the submit server is authorized to access, can be revoked by the client, and can have a time-limited validity. The "fcc problem" refers to delivering a copy of a message to a mailbox, and the most common case is a client leaving a copy of outgoing mail in a Sent Mail mailbox. The BURL extension can eliminate the extra transmission, since the final message is uploaded to the outgoing mailbox by the APPEND command; APPEND, including when enhanced by CATENATE, can only create a single copy of the message, and additional copies on the same server can be created with COPY commands.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally, forwarding an attachment means downloading the attachment to the phone and uploading it again. Here, the phone sends a reference instead, and the mail server fetches the attachment from the store itself. The reference carries a token that gives the submit server access to that one item and nothing else.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Implementors are advised to examine the security considerations of all the referenced documents. This section highlights the ones that arise from combining the extensions. The security considerations on forward without download are discussed throughout Section 8, and further considerations are found in the IMAP, Submission and Sieve documents.

On confidentiality of submitted messages, link protection such as TLS guards against an eavesdropper seeing the contents of a submitted message. Even without TLS the risk is no worse if BURL is used to reference the text than if the text is submitted directly: without BURL an eavesdropper gains the full text of the message, while with BURL the eavesdropper may or may not gain such access, depending on the form of BURL used, since some forms restrict use of the URL to an entity authorized as a Submission Server or a specific user.

On TLS, when a client uses BURL for submission, the extension requires sending a URLAUTH token to the mail Submission Server, and such a token should be protected from interception to avoid a replay attack that may disclose the contents of the message. TLS-based encryption of both the IMAP session that issues GENURLAUTH and the mail submission path provides that protection. Lemonade-compliant submission servers SHOULD use TLS-protected IMAP connections when fetching message content with the URLAUTH token, and when a client uses SMTP STARTTLS to send a BURL command that references non-public information, the submission server SHOULD use STARTTLS or an equivalent when fetching the content referenced by that URL, because the user expects the whole message to be treated confidentially.

The specification provides no security measures beyond those in the referenced documents, but it notes the risks associated with outband notifications, server configuration by client, client configuration by server, the presence of proxy servers, the presence of servers as intermediaries, the deployment models considered by the Open Mobile Alliance that are not conventional IETF deployment models, and measures to address a perceived need to traverse firewalls and mobile network intermediaries.
sections.plainLanguage: The token that lets the submit server fetch a message is itself a secret, so it must travel over an encrypted connection, and the fetch should also be encrypted. Without encryption, referencing a message with a URL is no worse than sending the text directly, and some forms of URL are restricted to a named server or user.

sections.title: Changes since RFC 4550
sections.content:
Compared with RFC 4550, the document adds requirements on a Lemonade compliant IMAP server: the extensions BINARY, COMPRESS=DEFLATE, CONTEXT=SEARCH, CONTEXT=SORT, CONVERT, ENABLE, ESEARCH, ESORT, I18NLEVEL=1, NOTIFY, QRESYNC, SASL-IR, SORT and URL-PARTIAL, and the keywords $SubmitPending and $Submitted. It also requires any Lemonade compliant IMAP server to support the CAPABILITY response code.

For Lemonade compliant Message Delivery Agents, the document adds support for the Sieve filtering language together with the Sieve extensions ENOTIFY, IMAP4FLAGS, RELATIONAL, VACATION and VARIABLES, and the comparator-i;unicode-casemap comparator. It recommends the DEFLATE compression method for TLS, and all other requirements remain the same.

Other changes and improvements to RFC 4550, which the RFC notes may be incomplete, are a new section with additional requirements on Lemonade Mail User Agents, in particular the requirement to support the Format=flowed parameter of the text/plain media type; a clarification of the use of the $Forwarded IMAP keyword; corrected and extended forward-without-download examples; and a new section describing in-band and out-of-band notifications from a Lemonade compliant mailstore.

For IANA, IMAP4 capabilities are registered by IETF Review as defined in RFC 5226. This document defines the URL-PARTIAL IMAP capability in Section 5.7.1, which IANA added to the IANA IMAP Capability registry.
sections.plainLanguage: The newer version of the profile demands more of the store and adds server-side filtering, which the earlier one did not require. It also adds one new IMAP capability, URL-PARTIAL, to the IANA registry.

viz.caption: THE IMAP EXTENSIONS THAT DO MOST OF THE WORK IN THIS PROFILE

items.title: CONDSTORE, QRESYNC, ENABLE
items.text: Let the client find out what changed since it last looked, so a dropped connection is cheap to recover from.

items.title: IDLE
items.text: Lets the store push news of a change in the selected mailbox instead of waiting to be polled.

items.title: NOTIFY
items.text: Lets the client ask for particular event types, such as a new message or a renamed mailbox.

items.title: ESEARCH, SORT, CONTEXT
items.text: Let the client search and sort without handling the whole mailbox, and return matches in a compact form.

items.title: BINARY
items.text: Moves decoding of message parts to the server, so less data crosses the link.

items.title: CONVERT
items.text: Lets the server convert a part to another media type, including scaling an image.

items.title: CATENATE
items.text: Builds a new message on the store from new text and parts already stored there.

items.title: URLAUTH, URL-PARTIAL
items.text: Hand out a URL that carries its own permission, so another server can fetch one named part.
